title: Exception Handling
intro: An exception is a run-time problem (dividing by zero, a missing file, a bad index) that interrupts normal flow. Java lets you throw, catch and propagate exception objects, so a program can recover instead of crashing.

cards.title: What is an exception?
cards.body:
The slides define an exception as a **run-time anomaly that a program may detect**. Examples: memory exhaustion, an input file that cannot be opened, division by zero.
When it happens, Java **creates an exception object** containing the type, a message and the program state, and **throws** it. The statements after that point are skipped unless the exception is handled.

cards.title: Before exceptions: if-checks and exit
cards.body:
AverageMarks V2 tests `if (numOfStudents <= 0)`, prints an error and calls `System.exit(0)`. This mixes error code with normal code, and the whole program ends.
V3 puts the normal code in a `try` block, `throw`s an Exception when the input is bad, and handles it in `catch`. Then **execution continues** after the try/catch.
keypoints: `throw new Exception("msg")` creates and raises an exception
`e.getMessage()` returns that "msg"
After the catch, normal flow resumes

cards.title: try / catch / finally: the template
cards.body:
**try**: statements that might throw. **catch (Type e)**: a handler, run only if a matching exception was thrown in the try. You may have several. **finally** (optional): runs **whether or not** an exception happened. Use it for clean-up such as closing files.
You must have at least one catch **or** a finally after a try.
keypoints: try needs a catch or a finally (or both)
finally runs in every case (unless System.exit)

cards.title: Flow of control: three scenarios
cards.body:
Trace which blocks run:
**No exception**: the whole try runs, all catches are skipped, finally runs, then the code after.
**Thrown and caught**: the try stops at the throw, the matching catch runs, finally runs, then the code after.
**Thrown, not caught here**: the try stops, no catch matches, **finally still runs**, and then the method ends immediately. The exception goes to the caller.

cards.title: The exception hierarchy (checked vs unchecked)
cards.body:
All exceptions are objects of subclasses of **Throwable**, which has two branches: **Error** (serious JVM problems) and **Exception**.
**Unchecked** = `RuntimeException` and its subclasses **plus `Error` and its subclasses**. Everything else under Exception is **checked**.

cards.title: Common unchecked exceptions and their causes
cards.body: These are the system-generated exceptions from the slides. Learn the line that causes each one:
cards.after: FileNotFoundException (a missing file) is a **checked** subclass of IOException. Note that `5.0 / 0` does not throw: double division gives Infinity.
keypoints: Index too big or negative: ...IndexOutOfBoundsException
Calling a method through null: NullPointerException
Integer divide by zero: ArithmeticException

cards.title: Checked exceptions: catch or declare
cards.body:
The compiler **analyses checked exceptions**. If a statement can throw a checked exception, the method must **either** catch it in try/catch **or** declare it with `throws` in its header. Doing neither is a **compile error**.
Unchecked exceptions need neither. If they are left uncaught, Java's default handler ends the program with the exception's name and stack trace.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
A["exception type X can be thrown"] --> B{"X is RuntimeException or Error, or a subclass?"}
B -- yes --> C["UNCHECKED: compiler does not force handling"]
B -- no --> D["CHECKED"]
D --> E["catch it with try-catch"]
D --> F["or declare: throws X in the header"]
D --> G["neither: COMPILE ERROR"]
keypoints: Checked: catch it or declare it with `throws`
Declaring passes the duty to the caller, which must then catch or declare
Unchecked: optional to handle

cards.title: throw vs throws
cards.body:
`throw` is a **statement** that raises one exception object right now. `throws` is a **clause in the method header** listing the exceptions the method may pass to its callers.
In the slides' AverageMarksV4, `computeAvgMarks() throws ArithmeticException` contains a `throw new ArithmeticException(...)`, and main catches it.

cards.title: Several catch blocks: the order matters
cards.body:
The catch blocks are tested **from top to bottom**, and **only the first one whose type matches** runs (a match includes subclasses, because of is-a). So put **specific** exceptions first and **general** ones (Exception) last.
If a superclass catch comes before a subclass catch, the later one can never run, and real Java reports a **compile error**.

cards.title: Propagation up the call stack
cards.body:
If an exception is **not caught** in the method where it happens, that method ends at once, and the exception is passed to the **method that called it**. This repeats until some caller catches it, or main lets it out and the program crashes.
The slides' ExPropagation: method3 throws, method2 has no handler, and method1 catches it.

cards.title: Useful methods of an exception
cards.body:
`Exception` has two constructors, `Exception()` and `Exception(String message)`, and these useful methods:
`getMessage()` returns the message. `toString()` returns the class name plus the message. `printStackTrace()` prints the chain of method calls that led to the exception.
keypoints: getMessage(): just the message
toString(): class name + ": " + message
printStackTrace(): which methods were active

cards.title: Creating your own exception class
cards.body: Extend an existing exception class. Extend `Exception` for a **checked** exception, or `RuntimeException` for an **unchecked** one. Usually you write only the constructors, which pass a message up with `super(message)`.
keypoints: extends Exception: checked (callers must catch or declare)
extends RuntimeException: unchecked
getMessage() returns the string passed to super(...)

cards.title: An exception thrown inside a catch block
cards.body: A catch block can itself throw (for example, to wrap an error in a new exception). The new exception is **not** handled by the **sibling** catch blocks of the same try; they only guard the try block. **finally still runs**, and then the new exception leaves the method.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body:
1. Thinking **Error is checked**. It is **unchecked**, like RuntimeException.
2. Thinking the rest of the try runs after the catch. It does not; execution continues **after the whole try/catch/finally**.
3. Expecting **several catches** to run. Only the **first match** runs.
4. Putting `catch (Exception e)` **first**. Then later catches are unreachable, which is a compile error.
5. Mixing up **throw** (a statement) and **throws** (in the header).
6. Forgetting that finally runs even when the exception is **not caught** (and even after `return`).
7. Calling a method that `throws IOException` without catching or declaring it.
keypoints: Error = unchecked
Only one catch runs; finally always runs
